title: 'A Nine-Member Committee Decided My Fate.' Manika Batra Is Done Fighting — For Now.
excerpt: India's most decorated table tennis player says TTFI broke its own constitution when it dropped her from the Asian Games squad. Now she says she's mentally exhausted and stepping back — but the questions she raised aren't going away.
body:
Manika Batra has been fighting the Table Tennis Federation of India for eleven days. On Thursday, she said she was done.

"I am mentally exhausted from this fight, and for now, I am putting my sword down," the three-time Olympian wrote on X. She wished the selected squad well and signed off with "Jai Hind."

But before she stepped back, she dropped one final allegation that may prove harder to dismiss than any of the others.

x-official:

The Constitutional Claim

Batra said the documents sent to her by the TTFI reveal that a nine-member selection committee decided the Asian Games team — while Article 24(C)(j) of the federation's own constitution states that no sub-committee can have more than seven members.

"A 9-member committee decided my fate, yet I am being told that the process was fully compliant with the Constitution and the rules," she wrote. "I will leave it to the people to decide, especially those who have repeatedly said that rules must be respected and followed equally by everyone."

The TTFI has maintained that the selection process was conducted "strictly in accordance with the rules." It has not publicly responded to Batra's specific constitutional claim about the committee's composition.

How She Got Here

The TTFI announced India's 10-member table tennis contingent for the 2026 Asian Games on June 18. The Games are scheduled for September 19 to October 4 in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. Batra — India's second-highest-ranked female player at World No. 51, behind Sreeja Akula at 45 — was named only as a reserve.

> **"I am asking for answers."

The TTFI responded that Batra's candidature was "specifically considered and voted upon by the selection committee," rejecting claims that she was not properly evaluated."**

The federation's selection policy, drafted in 2023, allocates 50 per cent weightage to national rankings, 40 per cent to world rankings, and 10 per cent to the discretion of the selection committee. Batra's problem is the first of those three: her absence from domestic tournaments left her without a national ranking, and that appears to have been the decisive factor.

But Batra sees the maths differently. She pointed out that she's only marginally outside the world top 50 — "a difference where movement in either direction can occur within a single ranking cycle" — and argued that a narrow miss on one component shouldn't override a decade of performance at the highest level. She also flagged what she described as inconsistency: in the previous Asian Games cycle, she said, players outside similar ranking thresholds were still included under "special considerations."

The PM Plea

Before the constitutional argument, Batra had already escalated. In a statement released on June 19, she wrote directly to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, requesting them to "look into the matter and ensure that the process is transparent, consistent, and fair to all athletes."

![Jai Hind — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/Netaji_Subhas_Chandra_Bose.jpg)

She made clear she wasn't asking to be put back on the team. "I am not asking to be selected. I am not asking anyone to overturn the decision. I am asking for answers."

The TTFI responded that Batra's candidature was "specifically considered and voted upon by the selection committee," rejecting claims that she was not properly evaluated. It was after that response that Batra raised the committee-size issue — shifting the argument from whether the decision was right to whether it was legal.

A Career of Firsts

The exclusion stings, in part, because of who is being excluded. Batra is arguably the most recognisable name in Indian table tennis. Born in Delhi in 1995, she won gold in both the singles and team events at the 2018 Commonwealth Games in Gold Coast — the first Indian woman to win a CWG singles gold in table tennis. She added a bronze in mixed doubles at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta, becoming the first Indian paddler to reach the singles quarterfinals at the continental games.

At the Paris Olympics in 2024, she became the first Indian table tennis player — male or female — to reach the Round of 16. She has represented India at three consecutive Olympics and remains one of the most followed Indian athletes on social media, with over 830,000 Instagram followers.

She is currently representing India at the WTT United States event, even as the federation row plays out.

The Bigger Picture

Batra's case is not happening in isolation. Indian sports federations have a long history of governance disputes — from the Wrestling Federation of India controversy that saw Olympic medallists protesting on the streets, to periodic conflicts in athletics, boxing, and hockey. Athletes have repeatedly struggled to get clear answers on selection criteria, and procedural compliance has often been an afterthought.

For Indian sports fans in the diaspora, the pattern is a familiar frustration. India's talent pipeline has never been deeper, but the structures around it — the committees, the policies, the communication — often feel like they belong to an earlier era.

Batra's sword may be down. But the question she raised — whether the people who pick India's teams are even following their own rulebook — isn't going anywhere.

---

India's Table Tennis Squad for Asian Games 2026:

Women: Sreeja Akula (c), Yashaswini Ghorpade, Diya Chitale, Sutirtha Mukherjee, Syndrela Das. *Reserves:* Swastika Ghosh, Manika Batra.

Men: G. Sathiyan (c), Harmeet Desai, Manav Thakkar, Manush Shah, Payas Jain. *Reserves:* Ankur Bhattacharjee, Ronit Bhanja.

*The Asian Games table tennis events will be held from September 20 to 28 in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.*
